opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that makes me optimistic is that robotics is finally starting to look like a problem where progress compounds. For a long time, every robotic system was kind of a bespoke engineering project: you'd build a specific machine for a specific task in a specific factory, and if anything about the environment changed, you'd have to re-engineer it. What's changing now is that we're seeing the beginnings of general-purpose robotic foundation models, systems that learn from lots of data across many different robots and tasks and can then be adapted to new settings much more cheaply. That shifts the economics completely, because the marginal cost of deploying a robot to a new task starts to go down rather than staying flat.

For the United States specifically, I think that matters a lot. One of the big stories of the last few decades is that a lot of physical production moved to places where labor was cheaper, and the U.S. kept the design and the software and the high-margin parts of the value chain. If you have robots that are genuinely flexible, that can handle the messy, variable parts of manufacturing, logistics, construction, agriculture, then labor cost stops being the dominant factor in where you put things. What matters is access to capital, to energy, to engineering talent, to the AI research ecosystem. And those are areas where the U.S. is actually quite strong.

I'd also push back a little on the framing that automation is purely about replacing people. If you look at what's actually happening, there are big parts of the economy that are labor-constrained: elder care, skilled trades, warehouse work, farming. There just aren't enough people willing or able to do those jobs at the scale we need. Robots that can take on the physically demanding, repetitive, or dangerous parts of that work could make those industries more productive and frankly make the remaining jobs better.

Now, I don't want to oversell the timeline. There's still a lot of hard research to do. Robots need to be much more reliable, they need to recover from mistakes, they need to generalize to situations they haven't seen. But the trajectory feels very similar to what we saw with language models a few years ago, where once you get the recipe right and you start scaling data, things improve faster than people expect. If that happens in the physical world, I think it could be one of the most significant drivers of economic growth we've seen in a long time, and the U.S. is well positioned to lead it.

r001.rationale: The response says robots could make labor-constrained industries more productive, but does not identify automation as multiplying output per hour of human work.

r002.rationale: It discusses robotics models, research, and deployment, but does not argue for balancing investment in software innovation with investment in hardware innovation.

r003.rationale: It names U.S. strengths in engineering talent and AI, but does not connect automation to an economy where highly educated people do high-value work as an incentive to pursue it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer starts with a kind of paradox. If you look at the US economy right now, there's this huge mismatch. On the one hand, we have enormous demand for physical work that isn't being met. Manufacturing can't fill positions, logistics is stretched thin, elder care is going to be a massive crunch as the population ages, agriculture is perpetually short on labor. And on the other hand, we have a lot of the structural ingredients that you'd want if you were going to solve that with technology. We have the research ecosystem, the capital, the compute, and increasingly the data. So the opportunity is real, and the question is whether the technology is actually ready.

What's changed in the last few years, and this is where my optimism really comes from, is that robotics has finally started to look like the rest of machine learning. For a very long time robotics was this island. You'd engineer a system very carefully for one task in one environment, and the moment anything changed, it broke. The methods didn't generalize, and they didn't scale with data the way vision or language did. That's no longer true. With foundation models for robots, what we're seeing is that you can train a single policy on a lot of diverse experience, across many robots, many tasks, many settings, and it starts to acquire broad competence. It can pick up a task it hasn't seen in a new kitchen, or a new warehouse, with relatively little additional data. That's the moment where robotics stops being bespoke engineering and starts being a scalable technology, and scalable technologies are what transform economies.

The other thing I'd say is that I don't think the story here is primarily about replacement. People tend to imagine robots as a one-for-one substitute for a worker, and in that framing it sounds zero-sum. But most of the value, especially early on, comes from doing things that currently just don't get done, or don't get done here. A lot of manufacturing left the US because the labor economics didn't work. If capable, adaptable robots make it viable to build things domestically again, that's not displacing American jobs, it's bringing an entire industrial base back, along with all the engineering, maintenance, and supply chain work around it. Same with care. We're not going to have enough caregivers for the number of elderly people we'll have in twenty years, no matter what. If robots can take on the physically demanding, repetitive parts of that, it lets the humans focus on the parts that actually require a person.

Now, I want to be careful not to be naive about this. There's a real gap between a compelling demo and a system that works reliably enough that a business will bet on it. Robots have to be safe around people, they have to be cheap enough, and they have to work in the long tail of weird situations that the real world throws at you. We're not there yet in most domains. But what makes me optimistic is that for the first time I can see a credible path from where we are to where we need to be, and it's the same path that got us here with language models: more data, more generality, better learning methods, and a feedback loop where deployed robots generate the experience that makes the next generation better. The US is unusually well positioned to run that loop. Whether we actually do it is more of a policy and investment question than a scientific one at this point, and that's a much better position to be in than we were in five years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots doing unmet work and letting people focus on human-centered tasks, but does not identify automation as increasing output per hour of human work.

r002.rationale: It mentions research, capital, compute, and data, but does not argue that building a robotics ecosystem requires balancing investment in software and hardware innovation.

r003.rationale: The response says robots could support domestic industry and free caregivers for work requiring people, but does not connect automation to an economy of highly educated people doing high-value work as an incentive.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics gives us a way to grow the economy that isn’t limited by how many people we have available to do particular jobs. If you want to build more housing, manufacture more goods, or take care of an aging population, ultimately somebody—or something—has to do that physical work. Progress in software is enormously valuable, but it doesn’t automatically remove those constraints.

What makes me optimistic is the possibility of making robots much more general. Traditionally, automation has required you to engineer a very specific system for a very specific task. That can work wonderfully in a factory producing millions of identical things, but it’s much harder to justify for a small business or an environment where things change every day. If robots can learn, and if the experience gained by one robot can help other robots, the economics could become very different.

For the United States, that could mean expanding what we’re able to produce domestically while making people more productive. A person who understands a manufacturing process could potentially oversee robots doing work that previously required a much larger operation.

I don’t think that means the transition will be painless, or that the benefits will distribute themselves automatically. Those are real issues. But the underlying opportunity is to make the things people need more abundant and less expensive. That’s a pretty compelling reason to try to get this technology right.

r001.rationale: It says robots could make people more productive, with one person overseeing work that previously required a much larger operation, conveying more output from human labor.

r002.rationale: It notes software progress and the potential of general robots, but does not argue for balancing investment in software and hardware innovation.

r003.rationale: It describes a person overseeing robots, but does not connect automation to an economy of highly educated people doing high-value work as an incentive for the United States.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reason to be optimistic is that robotics could let us produce a lot more with the people we already have. There are many things we would like to build, and many services we would like to provide, where the constraint is that there simply aren’t enough people available to do the work at a price that makes it feasible.

One way to think about automation is that you take an existing factory, replace the workers with robots, and make the same things a little more cheaply. But the more interesting possibility is that you make things possible that weren’t economical before. You can manufacture something domestically that otherwise wouldn’t be manufactured here. You can provide assistance to someone in their home who otherwise couldn’t afford it. That’s an expansion of what the economy can do.

And I think the United States has an opportunity because so much of the progress now depends on the intelligence of these systems. A robot doesn’t just need a good motor or a good gripper. It needs to understand what’s happening, adapt when something goes wrong, and learn new tasks without an engineer programming every little detail. If we can make progress on that, then the same physical machine becomes useful in many more settings.

That doesn’t mean the transition will be easy, or that every person benefits automatically. But the underlying opportunity is to increase productivity and make physical goods and services more abundant. That strikes me as a very substantial source of potential economic growth.

r001.rationale: It says robotics could let the U.S. produce more with its existing workforce and explicitly describes increasing productivity, conveying more output from available human labor.

r002.rationale: It mentions both system intelligence and physical components, but does not argue that building a robotics ecosystem requires balancing investment in software and hardware innovation.

r003.rationale: It discusses labor shortages and domestic production, but does not connect automation to a desired economy of highly educated people doing high-value work.
